title: Efficacy and Safety of Obinutuzumab in Active Lupus Nephritis
source: Science TLDR podcast episode 25 show notes
one_line: A phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled trial in 271 adults showed that adding the anti-CD20 antibody obinutuzumab to standard therapy improved complete renal response in active lupus nephritis at week 76.
key_claims: Complete renal response at week 76 was 46.4% with obinutuzumab vs 33.1% with placebo, a 13.4 percentage-point difference (p=0.02).
Treatment failure as an intercurrent event was lower with obinutuzumab (3.7% vs 17.6%).
Complete response with prednisone at or below 7.5 mg/day was 42.7% vs 30.9%, and UPCR <0.8 was reached by 55.5% vs 41.9%.
Death or renal events occurred in 18.9% of obinutuzumab patients vs 35.6% of placebo patients.

Serious adverse events were more frequent with obinutuzumab (32.4% vs 18.2%), mainly infections including COVID-19; excluding COVID-19, serious infections were 11% vs 7.6%, and there were 4 deaths (3 obinutuzumab, 1 placebo).
limitations: The COVID-19 pandemic confounded safety outcomes, with the trial starting before widespread vaccination.
Follow-up was limited to 76 weeks, leaving long-term renal and safety outcomes unknown.
All patients received mycophenolate mofetil plus prednisone, so results do not generalise to other background regimens.
No biomarker or subgroup analysis identifying which patients benefit most is reported in the notes.
open_questions: Does the renal response advantage persist and translate into preserved kidney function beyond 76 weeks?
How much of the excess serious infection risk disappears in a fully COVID-vaccinated population?
Which patients should be selected for B-cell depletion, and can biomarkers predict response?
Is obinutuzumab additive or superior when combined with or compared to other lupus nephritis therapies?
